title: Rarely categorical; highly separable representations along the cortical hierarchy.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Listed both author GitHub repos (realwsq/clustering-analysis, realwsq/brainwide-RRR-encoding-model; MIT licence). Downloaded data/mfr_all_conditions.pck (33.4 MB), checked its pickle opcodes (only numpy objects) and loaded it with a numpy-only unpickler: 29 cortical areas, 169 session-by-area blocks, 3,900 neurons, 16 task conditions (outcome x block prior x stimulus side x contrast), each a trials-by-neurons matrix of mean firing rates (median 939 trials per block). data/area_list.csv lists 43 cortical area acronyms. HEAD on the per-neuron selectivity file RRR_selectivity.json (Git LFS): 1,270,848,264 bytes, so not downloaded. Read the loading code: that file is a table with columns acronym, eid (session ID), RRR_r2, null_r2, RRR_beta (per-neuron coefficients, variables x time).
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The 14,000+ unit count and the 43-region total come from the abstract only; no full text in Europe PMC (paywalled, no PMCID). The columns of the 1.27 GB RRR_selectivity.json were inferred from the figure code, not from opening the file. That region labels come from histology-aligned probe tracks is known IBL (International Brain Laboratory) practice, not checked here. The README says the exact IBL data version used is available only by emailing the author.

a1_downloadable.note: Author repos are public on GitHub and IBL Brainwide Map data is public through the ONE API with no login. The exact data snapshot the authors used is 'contact us', but the derived files and the public source can be downloaded.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: For the obvious task (predict a neuron's cortical area), the area acronym is a column in RRR_selectivity.json (seen in code) and a dict key in the pickle (seen in file). Nothing has to be constructed.

a3_inputs_present.note: Per-neuron trial-wise firing rates by condition are in the pickle (checked); per-neuron encoding coefficients are in the 1.27 GB JSON (code only).

a4_units_stated.note: Pickle values look like firing rates in spikes per second (values 0 to about 27); units are not written in the file but follow from the code and IBL conventions. RRR coefficients are unitless model weights.

a5_enough_rows.note: 3,900 neurons in the 33 MB pickle, counted. The full selectivity table is said to hold 14,000+ units (abstract, not verified). That's enough for 29- to 43-way classification, but there are only 169 session-area blocks, which is the real unit for a held-out-session split.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: 33 MB pickle; 1.27 GB JSON needs a one-time streaming conversion
a6_fits_laptop.note: pandas.read_json on the 1.27 GB file could peak at several GB of RAM. Streaming it once into per-neuron arrays (14k x 9 variables x time bins) leaves well under 1 GB.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Pickle holds 3,900 neurons in 29 areas versus 14,000+ units in 43 areas in the abstract. This is consistent with the code's filters (encoding-model fit gain ΔR2 > 0.015, areas with ≥50 selective neurons), but the full-table count is unverified.

a8_label_provenance.note: Area label comes from anatomical localisation of the recording probe, not from a model of activity. The features (firing rates, encoding coefficients) are computed from spikes, not from the label.

B1.why: Pickle is nested dict area→session→condition; the JSON is one per-neuron table (from code). Few files, keys are clear.

B2.why: Python pickle (an unsafe format that needed a restricted loader) plus a 1.27 GB Git LFS JSON; neither is a clean CSV.

B3.why: One task and one pipeline (IBL standardised rig), processed uniformly by the authors.

B4.why: No censored values; firing rates are continuous and measured.

B5.why: Each neuron appears once per session block; no duplicates seen in the pickle.

B6.why: README and code comments explain the files; condition-key letters (W/S, 2/8, </>, l/h) had to be inferred.

C1.why: Asking 'does task selectivity add region information beyond intrinsic spiking?' gives an answer either way, but the effect is likely small.

C2.why: NEMO and Tolossa et al. decode region from spiking, both open with held-out-insertion or held-out-animal splits; neither uses task-selectivity features or fine cortical areas.

C3.why: Weak angle: fine-grained cortical areas from task encoding coefficients, and the paper already shows area selectivity tracks connectivity.

C4.why: Region assignment already comes from histology; decoding helps probe localisation only marginally.

C5.why: Majority-class and per-session baselines are obvious; NEMO reports 0.45 single-neuron accuracy on 10 broad IBL areas.

D1.why: NEMO (spike waveform + autocorrelation encoder) code is public; weight availability and licence weren't checked.

D2.why: NEMO needs waveforms and autocorrelograms from raw IBL spike data, which aren't in the derived files.

D3.why: Author repos are MIT licensed; IBL data are openly released.

E1.why: Hold out whole sessions (eid column in JSON per code; session blocks visible in pickle).

E2.why: 169 session-area blocks in the pickle; many areas have only 2–4 sessions, though.

E3.why: Majority-class and per-area mean firing-rate baselines are trivial to compute.

E4.why: No repeat recordings of the same neuron; noise ceiling for region decoding isn't estimable.

E5.why: Primary sensory areas (VISp, AUDp) are reported as categorical, so they should be the easiest to decode.

E6.why: Label shuffling and within-session shuffling are runnable.

E7.why: Allen Brain Observatory Neuropixels data and other IBL labs give independent recordings.

E8.why: Silhouette z-scores per area are saved in results.pk and reproducible from the pickle.

G1.why: Allen CCF (Common Coordinate Framework) area acronyms and IBL session IDs are standard keys.

G2.why: Full IBL Brainwide Map (621,733 neurons) and the Allen connectivity atlas (ctx2ctx_conn.csv in repo).

G3.why: Neuron→session and neuron→area joins are one-to-one.

G4.why: Combining with connectivity is what the paper already did; little new question left.

H1.why: All trials, including errors and both outcomes, are included (W/S condition keys).

H2.why: One mouse task, one species, many labs; cortex only.

H3.why: Claim is precise: decodes cortical area from task-encoding profiles of neurons with ΔR2 above 0.015 in the IBL task.

H4.why: Selection filters are visible in code; the dropped unselective neurons aren't discussed in what I could read.

I1.why: Systems-neuroscience groups (Fusi, Paninski, IBL) but no decision depends on it.

I2.why: A region decoder wouldn't redirect any experiment; histology already localises probes.

I3.why: Accuracy roughly matches a scientific question, not a decision.

I4.why: The paper shows linear readouts already work; nonlinear ML adds little.

J1.why: Mostly decoding and clustering analysis with little deep or transfer modelling.

J2.why: Needs systems-neuroscience intuition to judge area-decoding results.

J3.why: A reproduction of the silhouette results is shareable but not novel.

existing_models.name: NEMO (Yu et al., ICLR 2025): contrastive encoder of spike waveforms and autocorrelograms
existing_models.score_and_split: IBL Brainwide Map, 37,017 neurons, 10 broad brain areas, held-out insertions (70/10/20): single-neuron MLP accuracy 0.45, F1 0.42; multi-neuron 0.50 accuracy.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Ignores correlations between neurons; drops modality-specific information.

existing_models.name: Tolossa et al., eLife 2025: classifiers decoding anatomical location from spike trains
existing_models.score_and_split: Decodes region, structure and layer; reported to generalise across animals and labs (from search snippet; full text not retrieved, numbers not seen).

backbone.name: NEMO (neuron waveform + autocorrelogram encoder)
backbone.hardware: CPU for the head; generating inputs requires raw IBL spike-sorting outputs per session
backbone.licence: Author repos MIT; NEMO licence not checked

integration.partner_dataset: Full IBL Brainwide Map (621,733 neurons) plus Allen mouse connectivity atlas
integration.join_key: IBL session ID (eid) and Allen CCF area acronym
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Does a neuron's task-encoding profile identify its cortical area beyond what intrinsic spiking statistics already reveal? This only partly extends the paper's own connectivity analysis.

controls.positive_control: Primary sensory areas (VISp, AUDp, which the paper reports as categorical) should be decoded best; reproduce the per-area silhouette z-scores from results.pk.
controls.negative_control: Shuffle area labels within and across sessions; performance must drop to majority class.
controls.external_validation: Allen Brain Observatory Visual Coding Neuropixels recordings (different task, so only intrinsic-feature models transfer).

honest_claim_h3: Among IBL mouse cortical neurons whose responses are well fit by a task-encoding model, the profile of task-variable coefficients predicts the neuron's cortical area somewhat better than chance, and best in primary sensory areas.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use how a single cortical neuron responds to task events to predict which cortical area it was recorded from.
plain_idea.train_on: Per-neuron firing rates across 16 task conditions (or encoding-model coefficients for 9 task variables), 3,900 neurons verified in the small file and 14,000+ claimed in the large one.
plain_idea.predict: The neuron's cortical area (29 to 43 classes), taken from where the recording probe was anatomically located.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: It would show whether task responses carry area identity beyond intrinsic spike statistics; but region decoding from IBL spikes is already done, and the paper shows within-area responses are diverse.

more_or_better_data.why: NEMO used 37,017 IBL neurons; this paper's derived set is 3,900 (verified) to 14,000+ (claimed) neurons from the same IBL source.

confidence_score.why: No repeat recordings of neurons, so no per-prediction noise estimate; nothing here supports calibration beyond what any classifier gives.

models_beatable.why: NEMO (2025, contrastive encoder, held-out insertions) is recent and honest, but covers only 10 broad areas at about 0.45 accuracy; fine cortical areas are untested.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Adding task-selectivity coefficients to NEMO features would require recomputing NEMO inputs on the same neurons and split, and task coefficients may add nothing; no improvement holds by construction.

label_elsewhere.sources: IBL Brainwide Map (621,733 neurons, region-labelled; known resource) and Allen Brain Observatory Neuropixels (known resource)
label_elsewhere.why: Region labels exist for far more neurons, but those are the same data the existing models already used.

ml_idea: Predict a cortical neuron's area from its task-encoding coefficients (RRR betas) with session-held-out splits, and compare against intrinsic spiking features (NEMO-style) to ask whether task selectivity adds area information.

effort.compute_note: Estimated, not timed: the 33 MB pickle loads in seconds; the 1.27 GB JSON needs one streaming conversion; logistic regression on 14k x ~100 features runs in minutes.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Logistic regression on the 3,900-neuron pickle with session-held-out splits: if accuracy over 29 areas is near the majority baseline (beyond primary sensory areas), stop.

verdict_reason: Part A passes, but Part C fails (5/10). This is an analysis paper on the public IBL Brainwide Map, and its derived files add only per-neuron selectivity to data that NEMO and Tolossa et al. have already used for open, honestly split region decoding. The paper's own result (diverse, non-categorical responses within areas) predicts that a selectivity-based region decoder will be weak. No decision depends on the output, and the files are a pickle plus a 1.27 GB LFS JSON rather than a clean table.
